newsitem.title: USA: What economic data? Yankees fever boosts U.S. mkts.
newsitem.headline: What economic data? Yankees fever boosts U.S. mkts.

text.p: From the opening bell to the close of trade, financial markets were buoyed by Yankee victory fever on Tuesday.
Both bond and stock markets soared on the day New York City honored the Yankees' first World Series baseball championship in 18 years with a tickertape parade through the financial district.
Coupled with market-friendly economic news, the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond surged two full points and its yield fell to 6.68 percent, the lowest in almost six months.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 33 points.
No doubt the all around good markets day was helped by Yankees manager Joe Torre ringing the opening bell at the New York Stock Exchange.
"It was a Yankees rally," said a Treasuries trader. "It'll probably carry over until Election Day. The market now thinks (Bob) Dole is going to win."

If history is a guide, the Republican challenger should beat President Bill Clinton. The Yankees have played in five World Series coinciding with presidential elections. The three times the Yankees won, the Republican candidate did too. The two times the Yanks lost, the Democrats took the White House.
Like the Yankees, "Dole lost the first two games at home, but he'll win the next four, with three of them on the road," the trader predicted.
If that were to happen, it would be a bigger miracle than the Yankees' improbable comeback given Dole's place well behind Clinton in the polls.
Millions of fans packed lower Manhattan on Tuesday to celebrate the Yanks' stunning and thrilling win over the defending world champion Atlanta Braves.
Few of the fans that braved the crowds, though, were Wall Street types.
"I didn't see too many 'suits' when I was down there," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc, a lifelong Yankees' fan.
Though they stayed inside, above it all, "A lot of people were watching because a lot of us could see the parade from (our) buildings," he added.
Other Wall Street players admitted spending a lot of time either watching the parade from their offices or on TV.
And, contrary to the big drop in consumer confidence seen in October, street vendors were hawking T-shirts, hats, banners, and virtually every type of Yankees souvenir.
It seemed like there were vendors on every corner, but eager fans plunked down cash to buy Yankees' merchandise.

Some, though, weren't too concerned with the Yankees' celebration. "Wall Street had plenty of (other) reasons to rally on its own" without the parade, said David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities, a fan of the rival Cleveland Indians.

Indeed, the market was very active on Tuesday, helped by a tame Employment Cost Index. The ECI rose 0.6 percent in the third quarter -- below market expecations -- giving Treasuries more reason to believe no inflationary pressures are lurking.
The plunge in the Conference Board's consumer confidence index to 106.2 in October from September's 111.8 was also said to have contributed to the bond market's big rally.
"For an Orioles fan, the ECI was more relevant," said John Williams, chief global economist at Bankers Trust Co, an avid fan of the competing Baltimore team. "People knew to stay away from me."
